title: Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules
gist: The Trump-era FCC under Brendan Carr ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort rules against AT&T, clearing the way for AT&T to end copper landline service for about 199,000 customers on June 1, 2027 after a federal judge had rejected the same request. Democrat Anna Gomez dissented, and California may sue, extending a long federal-state telecom preemption fight.

insights.claim: The FCC ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, granting AT&T's preemption request after a federal judge had rejected AT&T's attempt to override the rules in court in July.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Regulatory relief obtained via the FCC after a court loss accelerates AT&T's copper retirement and cost-cutting in its largest holdout state.
insights.locator: The order released today granted AT&T’s request

insights.claim: AT&T plans to stop offering basic phone service to new California customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Copper decommissioning reduces legacy network maintenance costs; watch for timeline slippage if litigation follows.
insights.locator: AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort

insights.claim: California is the only state holding out against AT&T, which has received relief from COLR obligations in 20 of the 21 states in its wireline service territory.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: California is the final barrier to AT&T's full legacy copper exit across its wireline footprint.
insights.locator: The FCC order probably isn’t the last word

insights.claim: The FCC's COLR preemption order is unlikely to be final because California could sue the commission, prolonging uncertainty over AT&T's copper shutdown.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Litigation risk could delay AT&T's June 2027 discontinuance plans.
insights.locator: The FCC order probably isn’t the last word

insights.claim: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr argued California's 30-year-old COLR framework was designed for a bygone era and blocks AT&T from a federally authorized transition from legacy voice to IP-based alternatives.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Carr's FCC is signaling broad willingness to preempt state rules that slow legacy network retirement, a tailwind for incumbent telcos.
insights.quote: those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace
insights.locator: Carr: California rules “designed for a bygone era”

insights.claim: If AT&T ends copper service, many affected California homes and businesses would not be offered fiber; AT&T says a wireless home phone service on the cellular network is good enough, and the FCC agreed.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Substituting fixed wireless for copper lowers AT&T capex versus fiber overbuild but raises consumer-protection and political pushback.
insights.locator: If AT&T ends service on its old copper lines

insights.claim: California says wireless replacements are allowed if they meet state basic-service standards, including flat-rate unlimited voice, discounted Lifeline rates for low-income customers, and telephone relay service for deaf and hard-of-hearing people.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Defines the service obligations AT&T would otherwise need to meet in any wireless substitute.
insights.locator: California says its rules allow wireless replacements

insights.claim: FCC Democrat Anna Gomez voted against the order, arguing the CPUC has an open proceeding to modernize COLR rules and AT&T's own June 1, 2027 timeline leaves time for it to finish, so the FCC is treating the state regulator as an obstacle rather than a partner.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Dissent frames the legal and political case California could use in a challenge.
insights.quote: as an obstacle to be cleared

insights.claim: A March FCC order made it easier for carriers to discontinue copper networks and asserted that conflicting state rules are subject to preemption; AT&T cited that order in its lawsuit against California.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The March order is the legal foundation for broader federal preemption of state telecom rules benefiting all copper-retiring carriers.
insights.locator: In March, the FCC issued an order

insights.claim: The first Trump administration lost a 2019 attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws nationwide, and California later defeated ISPs in a court challenge to its net neutrality law.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Past federal preemption losses suggest the COLR order could also face meaningful legal risk.

insights.claim: California rejected US demands this month to stop enforcing its telecom laws, and may have to choose between enforcing them, including net neutrality, and receiving $1.42 billion in federal grants to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Federal broadband grant conditions are a pressure lever on state telecom regulation; watch impact on California broadband deployment funding.
insights.locator: California’s net neutrality law and other telecom regulations
